title: Benchmarking Optical Receivers for Quantum Communication and Randomness Certification
abstract: The choice of optical receiver determines which properties of the transmitted states remain visible in the observed data and therefore affects the performance of different quantum protocols. We compare continuous-variable, photon-counting and hybrid receivers within the same prepare-and-measure framework, using semi-device-independent randomness generation as the main case study. The measurement device is left uncharacterised, while the source is described by the Gram matrix of its pure signal states using an energy-derived overlap constraint, a magnitude-Gram benchmark or the full complex Gram matrix of a certified coherent phase-shift-keyed constellation. Within this framework, the observed receiver statistics are used to bound $H_{\min}(B|X,Λ)$ against classical side information correlated with the measurement device but independent of the input. For a fixed Gram matrix, this bound is obtained from an exact semidefinite program, with complex multi-input cases treated in block-real form and checked through the corresponding dual certificate. Photon counting alone is phase blind for fixed-modulus phase encoding and therefore certifies no worst-case randomness. Continuous-variable receivers give the highest certified entropy at moderate energy, while under the nominal source calibration a hybrid receiver performs better at low energy when the beacon-region label is retained in the output. The same receiver statistics also provide receiver-level comparisons for discrete-modulated continuous-variable quantum key distribution, quantum reading, covert communication and quantum-signature verification, without replacing the full security analysis required for each protocol.
summary: This paper rigorously benchmarks optical receivers—comparing continuous-variable, photon-counting, and hybrid detectors—to determine their impact on certified randomness extraction. Using SDPs, the authors show that receiver choice critically affects security bounds, demonstrating that hybrid schemes offer advantages at low energy while CV methods excel at moderate energy.
main_problem: The paper benchmarks how different optical receivers (CV, photon-counting, hybrid) affect the security analysis of quantum protocols, particularly for randomness certification.
main_result: Hybrid receivers perform optimally at low energy when retaining beacon labels, while continuous-variable receivers yield the highest certified entropy at moderate energies compared to other methods.
method: The authors use observed receiver statistics $P(b|x)$ within a prepare-and-measure framework to derive an exact bound on the min-entropy $H_{\min}(B|X, \Lambda)$ using Semidefinite Programming (SDP).
model_or_system: The system involves quantum states prepared by a source characterized by its Gram matrix and measured by uncharacterized optical receivers. The analysis is framed within semi-device-independent security proofs.
key_observables: $H_{\min}(B|X, \Lambda)$ (certified min-entropy), $P(b|x)$ (observed conditional probabilities), and the adversary's guessing probability ($P_{	ext{guess}}$).

main_assumptions: The security analysis assumes the side information $\Lambda$ is classical, and the source model is fixed by its Gram matrix or constrained by an energy bound.

paper_structure: The paper establishes the general framework using SDPs to bound min-entropy, analyzes specific receiver types (photon counting vs. CV/hybrid), derives quantitative results comparing their performance across energy regimes, and discusses implications for various quantum protocols.
why_interesting: It provides rigorous, information-theoretic bounds on achievable randomness in practical quantum communication settings by focusing on the measurement apparatus's limitations, which is crucial for designing robust quantum hardware.

figures.caption: Figure 1. General schematic of the protocol. A laser feeds the preparation stage, where the energy of the emitted state is bounded and monitored; the state is measured by an un- characterised device, and the raw outcomes are fed to post- processing, where the certified min-entropy determines the extractable randomness.

Figure 2. Detection schemes, labelled as in the panels. HD: homodyne, one quadrature by interference with a local oscil- lator. HT: heterodyne, both quadratures at the cost of an added vacuum unit. PNR: photon counting with multiplexed on–off elements. Hyb 1: beacon homodyne, conditional dis- placement, photon counting. Hyb 2 (Kennedy): nulling dis- placement and a single-photon detector.

Figure 3. Conditional laws P(b|x) for ternary PSK at µ = 0.2, ideal detectors–the exact matrices used as SDP input. PNR (multiplexed, Nbin = 20, click bins {0}, {1}, {2, 3}, {4–7}, {≥ 8}) is phase blind: its columns are identical, so Hmin = 0 by Proposition 1. Homodyne (P quadrature, midpoint bins), heterodyne (angular sectors) and Hybrid-1 (parameters of Sec. II E 5, beacon label traced out) produce input-dependent columns.

Figure 4. Hybrid-1 receiver. (a) General operating principle. A beacon homodyne measurement provides a coarse phase estimate, which determines the conditional displacement applied to the transmitted mode before photon-number-resolving detection. The panel gives a schematic phase partition rather than the precise ternary implementation. (b) Ternary implemen- tation. Two thresholds, T2 < T1, divide the beacon outcome into three regions associated with D(2gα), the identity operation and D(gα). The displaced amplitudes produce the branch- and input-dependent mean photon numbers λk,x of Eq. (37), which determine the corresponding PNR click distributions.

Figure 5(a) shows the certified entropy against µ in the coherent model. Homodyne rises from 0.35 bits at µ = 0.005 to its peak H⋆ min = 0.43 bits at µ⋆≈0.054 and falls back to 0.09 bits at µ = 1, where the constel- lation becomes too distinguishable to constrain the ad- versary; certification does not die at low energy because the bin edges scale with √µ, so the states approach each other exactly as fast as the data flatten. Heterodyne runs parallel and slightly below, while the Kennedy cas- cade and the coarse-grained Hybrid-1 remain substan- tially below the Gaussian receivers.
